## ACTIVE: A Dynamic Pareto-Frontier-Based Unified Index for Dual-Vector Query 

Shengyuan Lin 

Northeastern Univ., China linsy5847@gmail.com 

Shufeng Gong

ABSTRACT 

Existing approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) methods generally assume that each entity has a single vector. In many real-world applications, however, an entity is associated with more than one vector, and queries may jointly consider two attributes. With different queries assigning different weights to each attribute, Pareto-frontier-based indices provide an effective solution for dual-vector retrieval by connecting to approximate nearest neighbors under all possible query preferences. However, existing Pareto-frontier-based approaches suffer from substantial inefficiencies in both index construction and dynamic updates, limiting their practical applicability. To address these issues, we propose ACTIVE , a dynamic Pareto-frontier-based DVQ index that supports efficient construction and updates while maintaining high retrieval performance under vary-ing query preferences. It employs angle-constrained active-range computation and connectivity-loss-driven adaptive repair strategies to accelerate node insertion and deletion, respectively. Extensive experiments show that, at comparable (or slightly below) search accuracy, ACTIVE improves insertion throughput by 1 .20–1 .43 ×

over DEG, and deletion throughput by 1 .64–2 .06 × over neighbor-reconnection-based repair and by 22 .64–39 .51 × over reinsertion-based repair. 

1 INTRODUCTION 

Approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) over high-dimensional vectors has been widely adopted in applications such as recommendation systems [12, 34, 42, 43] and information retrieval [4, 33, 55, 65]. In these applications, the unstructured attributes of an entity, such as image, text, or audio, are embedded into vectors, and objects whose vectors are close (similar) to the query vector are retrieved. Traditional ANNS primarily focuses on single-vector retrieval [9, 16, 19, 22, 23, 30, 50, 59], i.e., entities are searched based on only one unstructured (vectorized) attribute. However, many real-world retrieval tasks require jointly consid-ering more than one vectorized attribute [5, 11, 32, 38, 39, 46, 48], with query-specific preferences assigned to each attribute. In this pa-per, we focus on dual-vector retrieval with exactly two attribute vec-tors, which is common in applications with complementary modal-ities, such as image–text of products on e-commerce platforms [20, 48, 61], spatial–textual data of posts on social platforms [11], and video–text of videos on short-video platforms [32, 61]. object is the weighted sum of their distances on the two vectors, where the query-specific preference determines the weight of each attribute distance. As query preferences vary, the distance between the same pair of entities changes accordingly, making efficient and accurate ANN retrieval particularly challenging. Furthermore, real-world datasets are inherently dynamic, with entities continuously being inserted and deleted. Such dynamic updates pose significant challenges to efficient index-based retrieval methods. 

Example 1: In product search on e-commerce platforms, consider two users who upload images of a smartphone and provide textual descriptions, such as “a smartphone with long battery life and excellent photography”. The first user aims to retrieve a smartphone that visually resembles the uploaded image, whereas the second user prioritizes the specific performance attribute. Accordingly, the first user assigns a larger weight to the image-vector distance, while the second user assigns a larger weight to the textual-vector distance when computing similarity based on the image and textual embeddings. Even when the two users provide the same phone image and textual description, different preferences can lead to different retrieval results. Meanwhile, vendors continuously update product listings due to inventory changes, ensuring accurate retrieval results for users. This makes the dynamic updating of dual-vector data indispensable. Thus, the DVQ problem requires efficient and accurate retrieval under arbitrary query preferences while also supporting efficient dynamic updates. 2

Motivation . Existing DVQ approaches [48, 49, 61, 63] mainly build graph-based ANNS indices over dual-vector data to enable efficient retrieval. However, they cannot simultaneously achieve high retrieval accuracy and high update efficiency. In general, these approaches can be divided into two categories. 

1) Preference-specific multi-indices. These approaches [48, 49, 63] build single-vector indices by fixing the query preference in advance. A representative solution is multi-index retrieval (MR) [48, 63], which builds a separate index for each attribute vector. It searches arXiv:2610.35751v1 [cs.DB] 26 Oct 2026 the two indices independently, merges the retrieved candidates, and subsequently reranks them by computing the exact weighted dis-tance. Since they assume that object distances are pre-determined, they suffer from limited retrieval quality under arbitrary query preferences, as shown in Figure 1a. 

2) Preference-agnostic unified indices. Unlike existing single-vector indices [16, 22, 30] that select similar vectors of each node as their neighbors, this approach [61] connects approximate nearest neighbors across all possible query preferences, ensuring that varying query preferences can be accommodated during search. To achieve this, approximate Pareto frontiers are utilized as the neighbors since they remain competitive under diverse preference settings, thereby enabling the selected neighbors to cover varying query preferences. As a result, Pareto-frontier-based indices provide a more suitable foundation for query-dependent similarity search in DVQ. However, existing unified indices do not support efficient dynamic updates because repairing Pareto frontiers is more complex than repairing neighbors in single-vector indices [28, 47, 62]. 

Our goal . In this work, we aim to design a dynamic Pareto-frontier-based DVQ index that supports efficient construction and updates while maintaining high retrieval performance. 

Challenges . Designing a preference-agnostic unified index is challenging for two main reasons. 

1) Expensive Edge Active-Range Computation in Construction. 

Pareto-frontier-based indices [61] select neighbors to cover different query preferences, but not every selected edge is useful under every preference. Thus, each edge needs to precompute its active ranges of the preference, allowing it to be traversed only when needed and avoiding redundant distance computations. Employing Relative Neighborhood Graph (RNG) pruning [61] enables the computation of such active ranges, however, its expensive time complexity introduces substantial additional computational overhead. Therefore, designing an efficient active-range computation method remains challenging. 

2) Inefficient Approximate Pareto Frontier Repair in Update. In Pareto-frontier-based indices, repairing the Pareto-frontier neigh-bors of affected nodes (i.e., in-neighbors of deleted nodes) after deletions is critical to preserving graph connectivity. Reinsertion-based global repair strategies [2, 30, 60] rediscover the neighbors of affected nodes by traversing from entry nodes, causing many distance computations and high update overhead. However, directly applying single-vector local repair strategies [47, 62] to Pareto-frontier-based DVQ indices is ineffective, as validated in Figure 1b and 1c, since they cannot guarantee that Pareto frontiers can be identified within the local neighborhood of DVQ indices. Therefore, designing an efficient repair strategy for approximate Pareto fron-tiers while maintaining high retrieval accuracy remains challenging. 

ACTIVE . The above challenges cannot be directly addressed by ex-isting techniques. Starting from these application-level challenges, we propose ACTIVE , a dynAmiC Pareto-fronTier-based unIfied DVQ indEx that supports dynamic updates while maintaining high retrieval quality under arbitrary query preferences. ACTIVE is built upon two techniques. To accelerate index construction, we introduce the Pareto angle and develop an angle-constrained active range computation algo-rithm, ACAR, based on the locality distribution of Pareto angles. In ACAR, each neighbor is compared only with other neighbors that satisfy the angle constraint under the triangle inequality. By restricting unnecessary comparisons, ACAR reduces construction overhead while preserving effective navigation quality of the DVQ index across diverse query preferences. For efficient updates, we observe a high overlap between the original neighbors and the repaired neighbors of affected nodes and introduce CA-PFR, a connectivity-loss-driven adaptive repair strategy that locally repairs approximate Pareto frontiers. We provide three methods, namely historical-Pareto-frontier, affected-layer, and multi-layer repair, according to the severity of connec-tivity degradation of affected nodes. This allows us to restore the connectivity of the graph without full re-insertion, significantly reducing distance computations and improving update throughput. In summary, the main contributions of this work are: 

• An observation of Pareto-angle locality motivates an angle-constrained active range computation algorithm, which accel-erates active range computation ( § 4). 

• An observation of high overlap between original and repaired neighbors of affected nodes motivates an incremental repair method. We propose a connectivity-loss-driven adaptive repair strategy, which locally repairs approximate Pareto frontiers according to the severity of connectivity degradation ( § 5). 

• Extensive experiments on diverse datasets show that ACTIVE 

achieves higher update throughput than state-of-the-art base-lines while maintaining a competitive trade-off between query accuracy and efficiency ( § 6). 

2 BACKGROUND AND MOTIVATION 

In this section, we first define the Dual-Vector Query (DVQ) problem and review Pareto-frontier-based DVQ index construction as well as update methods for single-vector graph-based indices. We then analyze their drawbacks and present the motivation of this work.

To address this, DVQ in practice retrieves 𝑘 approximate nearest results 𝑅 𝐷𝑉 𝑄 , achieving a trade-off between retrieval accuracy and search efficiency [21, 61]. To quantify the quality of the approximate results 𝑅 𝐷𝑉 𝑄 , recall [26, 51] is commonly used, defined as 𝑅𝑒𝑐𝑎𝑙𝑙 @𝑘 = |𝑅 𝐷𝑉 𝑄 ∩𝑅 𝑒𝑥𝑎𝑐𝑡 |

2.2 Pareto-Frontier-Based Index Construction 

Due to diverse query 𝛼 in DVQ, Pareto-frontier-based indices select the Pareto frontiers of each node as its out-neighbors, which can nearly cover the approximate nearest neighbors for all possible 𝛼 .

Pareto Frontier [29]. The construction of Pareto-frontier-based indices can be viewed as finding the Pareto frontier for each node. Given a node 𝑣 ∈ 𝑉 for which we aim to find its neighbors, each candidate node 𝑝 ∈ 𝑉 \ { 𝑣 } induces a distance pair relative to 𝑣 ,␀𝛿 𝑥 (𝑣, 𝑝 ), 𝛿 𝑦 (𝑣, 𝑝 ). For any 𝑝, 𝑞 ∈ 𝑉 \ { 𝑣 }, we say that 𝑝 dominates 

𝑞 , denoted by 𝑝 ≺ 𝑞 , if and only if (1) ∀𝑖 ∈ { 𝑥, 𝑦 }, 𝛿 𝑖 (𝑣, 𝑝 ) ≤ 𝛿 𝑖 (𝑣, 𝑞 ),and (2) ∃𝑗 ∈ { 𝑥, 𝑦 }, 𝛿 𝑗 (𝑣, 𝑝 ) < 𝛿 𝑗 (𝑣, 𝑞 ). The Pareto frontier of 𝑣 is defined as 𝑃𝐹 𝑣 ⊆ 𝑉 \ { 𝑣 }, where ∀𝑝 ∈ 𝑃𝐹 𝑣 , ∄𝑞 ∈ 𝑉 \ { 𝑣 }, 𝑞 ≺ 𝑝 , i.e., the neighbors of 𝑣 in 𝑃𝐹 𝑣 cannot be dominated by any node. 

Multi-layer Pareto Frontiers . In Pareto-frontier-based indices, only using the Pareto frontier of each node as its out-neighbors leads to an extremely sparse graph index. This is because, in a dataset with millions of objects, the size of the Pareto frontier is typically small (e.g., the average size is 8.26 on CC3M) , while hundreds of candidate nodes are usually required to select as the final out-neighbors. To address this, the multi-layer Pareto frontiers 

{𝑃𝐹 1

𝑣 , . . . , 𝑃𝐹 𝑙 𝑣 } are selected as the candidate out-neighbors of each node 𝑣 , where 𝑙 is the number of layers bounded by the candidate pool size 𝑒 𝑓 𝑐𝑜𝑛𝑠𝑡𝑟𝑢𝑐𝑡 , as shown in Figure 2b. Neighbors in the first layer correspond to the global Pareto frontier. Each subsequent layer is recursively constructed by removing the current Pareto frontier and extracting a new Pareto frontier from the remaining candidates, referred to as FindPF [7]. 

Approximate Pareto Frontier Search . However, the construction of exact multi-layer Pareto frontiers is computationally expensive, as it requires computing distances to all other nodes in the dataset for each node. Therefore, approximate Pareto frontiers are typically used as candidate neighbors for each node, which are constructed using the Greedy Pareto Frontier Search (GPS) to expand candi-date neighbors layer by layer (see Algorithm 1). Specifically, GPS iteratively expands unexplored nodes in the lowest layer of Pareto frontiers containing them until no unexplored nodes remain. Finally, the candidate set C is selected as the approximate Pareto frontier.

To accelerate query processing, we assign preference intervals (i.e., active ranges ) to each edge, enabling the system to selectively traverse only the edges whose active ranges include the query 𝛼 . However, computing the active ranges of each edge is difficult [61]. DEG adopts an RNG-inspired pruning strategy similar to those used in single-vector graph indices. Specifically, for each candidate neighbor in C corresponding to an outgoing edge, it evaluates the distance to every other candidate neighbor and computes an interval of the parameter 𝛼 over which the edge becomes the longest edge in the corresponding triangle configuration. The active range is then obtained by excluding all such intervals from the complete parameter domain [0, 1]. This method requires comparing each neighbor of a node with all retained neighbors to determine its active ranges, resulting in a time complexity of 𝑂 (𝑅 · |C|) , where 𝑅 is the maximum out-degree. 

Summary . Existing Pareto-frontier-based DVQ index construction methods still face performance challenges, as the active range computation introduces substantial computational overhead. 

2.3 Pareto-Frontier-Based Index Updates 

In real-world scenarios, timely updates of indices are essential for search accuracy. Although no specialized DVQ index has yet been proposed to efficiently support dynamic updates, especially for node deletions, existing update techniques for single-vector graph-based indices are already well-established [2, 47, 60, 62]. Next, we review representative update methods in existing single-vector graph-based indices. The insertion procedure can follow the same logic as the construction process. Therefore, we focus our discussion on the deletion case. Existing repair strategies can be broadly classified into the following two categories: 1) Reinsertion-Based Repair (RBR) meth-ods [2, 30, 60] treat affected nodes as newly inserted nodes and reinsert them to reconstruct their out-neighbors. Although these methods can maintain high index quality, the global search in-curs significant computational overhead. 2) Neighbor-Reconnection-Based Repair (NRBR) methods [47, 62] restore graph connectivity through local reconnections, based on the intuition that neighbors of neighbors are likely to remain close to the affected node. Com-pared with RBR, NRBR may degrade index quality while achieving higher update throughput. However, in Pareto-frontier-based DVQ indices, these NRBR methods cannot guarantee that the neighbors of a node’s neighbors belong to its Pareto frontiers, making it difficult to maintain high retrieval accuracy. 

Summary . Update strategies for single-vector graph indices pro-vide useful insights for DVQ index updates. For instance, the

Limitations . Based on the analysis in Section 2.2 and 2.3, existing Pareto-frontier-based DVQ indices suffer from inefficient index construction and substantial update overhead. 

3 OVERVIEW 

To overcome the above limitations, we design ACTIVE , as shown in Figure 3. To accelerate index construction, 1) we introduce an angle-constrained active range computation (§4) strategy that avoids comparing each candidate neighbor against all retained neighbors by leveraging angular constraints. To accelerate index updates, 2) we propose a connectivity-loss-driven adaptive repair 

(§5) strategy that locally repairs the approximate Pareto frontiers of affected nodes according to the severity of their connectivity degradation. Furthermore, we incorporate asynchronous reverse graph maintenance to efficiently locate the affected nodes ( §5.2). 

Index Construction . ACTIVE employs an incremental construction strategy for each object in the dataset. Specifically, when construct-ing the out-neighbors of node 𝑣 , the candidate set C is obtained by performing greedy Pareto frontier search over the current index. Subsequently, ACTIVE computes the active ranges of nodes in C

using the proposed ACAR and selects the top-𝑅 unpruned neighbors in lower layers of Pareto-frontiers as the final out-neighbors 𝑁 out (𝑣 ).Finally, for each 𝑣 ′ ∈ 𝑁 out (𝑣 ), a reverse edge (𝑣 ′, 𝑣 ) is added to guarantee reachability of 𝑣 during subsequent searches. 

Index Update . For insertion, ACTIVE adopts the incremental con-struction approach to add new nodes into the graph index. For deletion, ACTIVE first leverages reverse graph topology to quickly locate the affected nodes. Then, ACTIVE adaptively repairs the af-fected nodes with three methods, namely historical-Pareto-frontier repair, affected-layer repair, and multi-layer repair, according to the severity of connectivity degradation for each affected node. Finally, 

ACTIVE computes the active ranges of the candidate neighbors for each affected node and selects the resulting final neighbors. 

Dual-Vector Query . For a given dual-vector query 𝑞 and a query preference 𝛼 , ACTIVE performs the greedy search based on the distance function (i.e., Eq.1) to obtain the top-𝑘 approximate nearest neighbors. Specifically, ACTIVE maintains a candidate queue 𝑄 𝑐 

and a result queue 𝑄 𝑟 , where 𝑄 𝑐 contains the visited but not expanded nodes while 𝑄 𝑟 contains the expanded nodes, both ordered by their distances to the query. At each iteration, the <latexit sha1_base64="26ABzLvs+7KAcmVPb+iHEbyGJHk="></latexit>

4 ANGLE-CONSTRAINED ACTIVE RANGE COMPUTATION 

The workflow reveals that active range (AR) computation is invoked during both index construction and updates. This additional over-head substantially degrades both construction and update efficiency. To reduce this cost, we exploit the visited characteristics of Pareto-frontier-based neighbors and introduce an angle-constrained AR computation algorithm that improves computational efficiency. 

4.1 Pareto Angle 

The existing AR computation algorithm [61] computes the active ranges of the candidate set C of a node in a nested-loop manner. The forward traversal order of C follows a two-level sorting scheme : nodes are first ordered by the layer of the Pareto frontiers in ascending order and then sorted within each layer 𝑃𝐹 by their dis-tance to 𝑣 along a given dimension (e.g., 𝛿 𝑥 (𝑣, ·) ). Specifically, when processing node 𝑣 , DEG sequentially traverses its out-neighbors 

(𝑎, 𝑏, 𝑐, 𝑑, 𝑒, 𝑓 , . . . ) to compute their active ranges, following a two-level order: from lower to higher Pareto-frontier layers (i.e., layer 1 to 𝑙 ), and within each layer in ascending order of 𝛿 𝑥 (𝑣, ·) , i.e., from node 𝑎 to 𝑒 as illustrated in Figure 4. When traversing node 𝑓 , DEG compares it against all previously retained nodes, i.e., 𝑎 −𝑒 . However, this strategy performs redundant comparisons for each candidate neighbor. For 𝑓 , it is unnecessary to compare 𝑓 with 𝑒 , since 𝑓 

is close to the 𝛿 𝑦 (𝑣, ·) axis while 𝑒 lies closer to the 𝛿 𝑥 (𝑣, ·) axis, making it highly unlikely that they will be simultaneously retrieved during query processing. Before introducing our AC computation method, we first introduce Pareto Angle. Definition 1 (Pareto Angle ( 𝜙 )). Given a node 𝑣 and its out-neighbor 𝑐 , the Pareto angle 𝜙 (𝑣, 𝑐 ) is defined in the 2D space induced by (𝛿 𝑥 (𝑣, 𝑐 ), 𝛿 𝑦 (𝑣, 𝑐 )) . We define 

𝜙 (𝑣, 𝑐 ) = arccos (𝛿 𝑥 (𝑣, 𝑐 ), 𝛿 𝑦 (𝑣, 𝑐 )) · ( 0, 1)√︁

and the positive 𝛿 𝑦 (𝑣, ·) -axis. The value of 𝜙 (𝑣, 𝑐 ) lies in [0, 𝜋 /2].

Observation . We construct Pareto-frontier-based indexes on three real-world datasets, OI, HM, and CM (details in Table 1), with all edges assigned an active range of [0, 1]. We perform a search under query 𝛼 = 0.1 and obtain the result queue 𝑄 𝑟 for each query, which contains the 𝑒 𝑓 𝑠𝑒𝑎𝑟𝑐ℎ closest retrieved nodes. We further compute the Pareto angle 𝜙 (𝑣, 𝑟 ) for each retrieved node 𝑟 ∈ 𝑄 𝑟 , where 𝑣 is 

4the in-neighbor that triggers the insertion of 𝑟 into the candidate queue during the expansion of 𝑣 . After the search, we count the frequency distribution of all retrieved nodes across different cosine values cos (𝜙 ), as shown in Figure 5. From Figure 5, we make the following key observation: 

Pareto-Angle Locality . Retrieved nodes exhibit strong locality in the Pareto angle space, where high-frequency Pareto angle regions form contiguous intervals. For instance, when 𝛼 = 0.1, nodes with higher retrieval frequency are mainly distributed in the range of cos (𝜙 ) ∈ [ 0.2, 0.4].

Intuition . Based on the observation, it is unnecessary for each neighbor to be compared against all other neighbors when com-puting its active range. Instead, comparisons should be restricted to neighbors with small differences in Pareto angle values. This is because such neighbors are more likely to be jointly retrieved under a given preference parameter 𝛼 , and hence jointly participate in forming triangles with the target node during graph traversal. 

4.2 Active Range Computation Based on Pareto Angle Difference 

Based on the above intuition, we propose an angle-constrained active range computation algorithm, ACAR , which leverages the Pareto angle constraint to avoid unnecessary distance computations. The core idea of ACAR is that, for any two candidate neighbors 𝑒 

and 𝑓 of a node 𝑣 , if both are retrieved during the search under a given 𝛼 , the absolute difference between their Pareto angles, i.e., 

|𝜙 (𝑣, 𝑒 ) − 𝜙 (𝑣, 𝑓 )| , should be constrained in a scope. Specifically, when computing the active ranges of a node’s can-didate neighbors, ACAR employs different strategies for candidates in the first Pareto-frontier layer and those in the remaining layers, as shown in Algorithm 2. This is because nodes in the first layer are more likely to lie on the exact Pareto frontier, and thus require more precise active range computation. 

(1) The First Layer . In DEG, the first traversed node is assigned an active range of [0, 1] simply because the neighbor set 𝑁 𝑆 is initially empty, which is clearly inaccurate. More importantly, the active range computation for nodes in the remaining layers depends on the active ranges of nodes in the first layer, making the accuracy of the first-layer active ranges crucial. To address this, ACAR employs a bidirectional two-stage scan over the first-layer candidate neighbors to compute more accurate active ranges. Specifically, in the first-stage scan, ACAR traverses the first-layer candidate neighbors in forward order to obtain the most reliable active ranges of the final retained node in 𝑁 𝑆 (line 4). After completing the forward scan, we perform a reverse scan with the same pruning operations (line 5), refining the active ranges of the first-layer neighbors. 

(2) The Remaining Layers . Since the proportion of candidate neigh-bors in the first layer is relatively small (only 4.53% on the OI dataset), the majority of the computational cost during the AR computation is incurred by computing the active ranges of can-didate neighbors in the remaining layers. When computing the active ranges of each neighbor, DEG compares it with all nodes currently retained in 𝑁 𝑆 , which leads to substantial computational overhead. To address this, inspired by the observation in Section 4.1, ACAR leverages a Pareto angle threshold 𝜃 𝑡ℎ ∈ [ 0, 𝜋

5 CONNECTIVITY-LOSS-DRIVEN INCREMENTAL PARETO FRONTIER REPAIR 

As discussed in Section 2.3, applying single-vector repair methods for DVQ indices that incorporate Pareto frontiers is unable to simul-taneously ensure update efficiency and retrieval effectiveness. To address this issue, we introduce a connectivity-loss-driven adaptive repair algorithm to maintain graph connectivity under deletions while avoiding unnecessary repair operations. 

5.1 Observation & Intuition 

For each affected node, reinsertion-based repair (RBR) methods per-form Greedy Pareto Frontier Search from entry nodes to reconstruct its candidate neighbors. However, reinsertion incurs substantial redundant computations, resulting in inefficient updates. 

Observation . To investigate the feasibility of incremental repair in Pareto-frontier-based indices under deletions, we measure the out-neighbor overlap ratio of affected nodes on three real-world datasets, as shown in Figure 7a. Specifically, we compute the overall overlap ratio of the out-neighbors for each affected node

𝑜𝑢𝑡 (𝑣 ) denote the out-neighbor sets before and after reinsertion, respectively. Further-more, we analyze the overlap ratio across different layers of Pareto frontiers. Here, affected layers refer to layers that contain deleted nodes (i.e., layer 2). Low layers are defined as all layers below the lowest affected layer (i.e., layer 1), while high layers refer to the affected layers and all layers above them (i.e., layer 2 and layer 3), as illustrated in Figure 7b. We observe that 1) the overall overlap ratio is at least 72% , indicating that most original neighbors remain effective after repair , and 2) 87% of neighbors in low layers are preserved, whereas only 52% in high layers are retained .

Intuition . These observations provide strong support for incremen-tal repair, which avoids the costly global search over all neighbors required by the reinsertion-based method. Observation 1) suggests OI HM CM Datasets 0.4 0.6 0.8 1.0 Nbr. Overlap Ratio

5.2 Pareto Frontier Repair Based on Connectivity Loss 

We further analyze the distribution of deleted neighbors among affected nodes under a 1% deletion batch on the OpenImage index, with a maximum neighbor size of 𝑅 = 40. The results show that the number of deleted neighbors varies significantly across affected nodes (i.e., in-neighbors of deleted nodes), ranging from 1 to 20, indicating that the degree of connectivity loss induced by deletions differs substantially among affected nodes. We next provide a formal definition of connectivity loss. Definition 2 (Connectivity Loss (CL)). The connectivity loss of a node 𝑣 measures the number of its lost out-neighbors, and its degree is defined as 

CL (𝑣 ) ≜ 𝑅 − | 𝑁 𝑜𝑢𝑡 (𝑣 )| 

𝑅 , (3) 

where 𝑅 denotes the maximum number of neighbors and 𝑁 𝑜𝑢𝑡 (𝑣 )

denotes the current out-neighbor set of 𝑣 . It holds that CL (𝑣 ) ∈ [ 0, 1].

Ideally, each node in the index maintains 𝑅 out-neighbors, result-ing in no connectivity loss (CL = 0). In practice, due to imperfect construction or deletions, nodes may suffer from connectivity loss. To this end, we categorize the degree of connectivity loss into three levels, mild, moderate, and severe. Specifically, for a node 𝑣 ,mild connectivity loss corresponds to CL (𝑣 ) ∈ [ 0, 𝐶𝐿 1], moderate connectivity loss corresponds to CL (𝑣 ) ∈ ( 𝐶𝐿 1, 𝐶𝐿 2], and severe connectivity loss corresponds to CL (𝑣 ) ∈ ( 𝐶𝐿 2, 1], where 𝐶𝐿 1 and 

𝐶𝐿 2 are the connectivity loss thresholds. 

Connectivity-Loss-Driven Adaptive Repair . Based on the above analysis, we design a connectivity-loss-driven adaptive Pareto frontier repair algorithm, CA-PFR, to restore the connectivity of the graph index. The core idea of CA-PFR is to determine the repair intensity for affected nodes according to the degree of connectivity loss. The detailed procedure of CA-PFR is shown in Algorithm 3. Specifically, when a set of nodes D is deleted, CA-PFR repairs the affected nodes 𝑉 𝑎𝑓 𝑓 𝑒𝑐𝑡𝑒𝑑 , i.e., the in-neighbors of the deleted nodes, according to their degree of connectivity loss. For each affected node 

𝑣 ∈ 𝑉 𝑎𝑓 𝑓 𝑒𝑐𝑡𝑒𝑑 , CA-PFR first organizes its out-neighbors into multi-layer Pareto frontiers C = {𝑃𝐹 1

𝑣 , . . . , 𝑃𝐹 𝑙 𝑣 } (line 2), and then obtains its active out-neighbors 𝑂𝑢𝑡 ← 𝑁 𝑜𝑢𝑡 (𝑣 ) \ D (line 4) and active in-neighbors 𝐼𝑛 ← 𝑁 𝑖𝑛 (𝑣 ) \D (line 5). Next, the degree of connectivity loss for node 𝑣 , CL (𝑣 ), is computed (line 6) according to Definition 2. Based on CL (𝑣 ), CA-PFR adopts historical-Pareto-frontier repair,

Historical-Pareto-Frontier Repair . The candidate set C′ consists of 

𝑣 ’s active out-neighbors 𝑂𝑢𝑡 and active in-neighbors 𝐼𝑛 (line 8). Due to the low connectivity loss, this strategy leverages the in-neighbors of affected nodes to efficiently reduce connectivity degradation with minimal overhead. In particular, it avoids any distance computa-tions during candidate selection, thereby significantly reducing the overall repair cost. The key idea is that, due to the reverse edges introduced during index construction, the in-neighbors of a node have previously served as its candidate out-neighbors. 

Affected-Layer Repair . The candidate set C′ consists of 𝑂𝑢𝑡 , 𝐼𝑛 ,and an additional expanded set 𝑂𝑢𝑡 2 derived from the affected layers of Pareto frontiers (i.e., layer 2 in Figure 7b). Specifically, CA-PFR first locates the affected layers in C that contain deleted nodes, denoted by C𝑎𝑓 𝑓 𝑒𝑐𝑡𝑒𝑑 (line 10). It then expands the nodes in these affected layers to form the expanded set 𝑂𝑢𝑡 2 (line 11). This expansion strategy is motivated by the observation that neighbors in layers below the affected layers are rarely updated during repair. By expanding nodes in these affected layers, CA-PFR can effectively restore local connectivity while avoiding unnecessary exploration. 

Multi-Layer Repair . The candidate set C′ consists of 𝑂𝑢𝑡 , 𝐼𝑛 and an expanded set 𝑂𝑢𝑡 2 derived from all high layers (i.e., the "High" region in Figure 7b). Specifically, CA-PFR first locates the lowest affected layer containing deleted nodes and denotes its layer ID as 

ℓmin (line 14). It then collects all layers of Pareto frontiers whose layer IDs are not smaller than ℓmin , denoted by Cℎ𝑖𝑔ℎ (line 15), and gathers the active out-neighbors of nodes in these layers to form 𝑂𝑢𝑡 2 (line 16). This expansion strategy is designed not only to address significant connectivity loss caused by deletions, but also to mitigate connectivity deficiencies inherited from the index construction phase, thereby further improving overall graph connectivity. Example 3: To better illustrate how CA-PFR adaptively repairs the in-neighbors affected by a deleted node, we focus on the case of severe connectivity loss, corresponding to node 𝑣 7, as shown in Figure 8. For the affected node 𝑣 7, CA-PFR first computes its connectivity loss CL (𝑣 7) = 3/4. Since CL (𝑣 7) exceeds 𝐶𝐿 2 (i.e., 1/2), CA-PFR classifies 𝑣 7 as exhibiting severe connectivity loss and thus triggers the multi-layer repair strategy. Specifically, CA-PFR employs Multi-Layer Repair to construct the final candidate set, i.e., 𝑣 0, 𝑣 2, 𝑣 3, 𝑣 4, 𝑣 5, 𝑣 6. Finally, node 𝑣 7 connects to 𝑣 0, 𝑣 4, 𝑣 5 and 𝑣 6

after the AR computation, as shown in Figure 8c. Notably, this strategy compensates for inherent connectivity deficiencies in the initial index. For example, in the initial graph index (see Figure 2a), reaching 𝑣 4 from 𝑣 3 follows the path 𝑣 3 → 𝑣 7 → 𝑣 2 → 𝑣 4 (3 hops). In contrast, after multi-layer repair (see Figure 8c), 𝑣 3 can reach 𝑣 4

via 𝑣 7 in only 2 hops, thereby reducing search latency. 2

Asynchronous Reverse Graph Maintenance . During deletion, 

ACTIVE requires in-neighbor information to locate and repair af-fected nodes. Since the graph-based index stores only out-neighbors, obtaining in-neighbors would otherwise require scanning the entire graph topology 𝐺 𝑜𝑢𝑡 . To avoid this overhead, ACTIVE maintains a lightweight reverse graph topology 𝐺 𝑖𝑛 , where for each node 

𝑣 , 𝑁 𝐺 𝑖𝑛 

𝑜𝑢𝑡 (𝑣 ) = 𝑁 𝐺 𝑜𝑢𝑡 

𝑖𝑛 (𝑣 ). Unlike 𝐺 𝑜𝑢𝑡 , whose edges store dual-vector distances and active ranges, 𝐺 𝑖𝑛 stores only in-neighbor IDs, accounting for merely 2.34% of the combined size of 𝐺 𝑜𝑢𝑡 

and the dual-vector data in the HM dataset. Since batch updates modify edges in 𝐺 𝑜𝑢𝑡 , ACTIVE asynchronously maintains 𝐺 𝑖𝑛 in the background to minimize synchronization overhead. 

Distance Storage and Memory Overhead . In ACTIVE , we store only the distances between each node and its neighbors with respect to the two attribute vectors as edge metadata in the adjacency list, which are reused during historical-Pareto-frontier repair and active range computation. When an edge is accessed, its distance values can be read in the same memory access without an additional lookup. During index updates, these distances are inserted or removed together with the edge metadata. Despite the modest additional storage overhead , this design improves update throughput and is therefore practically meaningful. For fairness, all baselines also store dual-vector distances in Section 6.

Therefore, the computational complexity for repairing an affected node 𝑣 is 𝑂 (| ΔC|) , where ΔC = C′ \ C denotes

6 EVALUATION 6.1 Experimental Setup 

Evaluation Platform . All experiments are conducted on a server with an Intel(R) CPU, 320 GB memory. The system runs Ubuntu 22.04 LTS with GCC version 11.4.0. 

Datasets . We evaluate our system on five publicly available real-world datasets, namely OpenImage (OI) [61], Howto100M (HM) [61], CC3M (CM) [61], LAION (LN) [44] and Caselaw (CW) [3], as summarized in Table 1. For CW, we construct its DVQ version using the original single text embeddings and associated court location metadata. Note that ACTIVE is not restricted to the attribute-type combinations in Table 1, but generalizes to arbitrary dual-vector data types. 

Compared Methods . We comprehensively evaluate ACTIVE 

against baselines to validate its search and update performance.

ACTIVE 732.33 1351.25 2539.33 6902.11 16220.81 

Static Search . We select multi-index retrieval (MR) [48, 63] and DEG [61] as baselines for static search, where MR builds a separate single-vector index (i.e., an HNSW index) for each of the two attribute vectors. The difference between ACTIVE and DEG in construction lies in their active range computation methods. 

Dynamic Updates . Since no dedicated methods exist for dynamic DVQ index updates, we use RBR [60] and NRBR [47] for deletions and DEG’s incremental construction strategy for insertions. These baselines employ existing AR computation algorithms [61]. 

Parameter Settings . During index construction, we set 𝑒 𝑓 construct =

200 and 𝑅 (or 𝑀 ) = 40 for ACTIVE , DEG and MR. On LN, 𝑒 𝑓 construct 

is increased to 400, because setting them to 200 yields an average out-degree of only about 𝑅 /2 due to the data distribution. The other parameters for DEG and MR follow those recommended in their respective papers. The Pareto angle threshold of ACTIVE is set to 

𝜃 𝑡ℎ = 𝜋 /18. During updates, we set 𝑒 𝑓 update = 100 for insertions in 

ACTIVE and DEG, and for reinsertions in RBR, and use 𝑒 𝑓 search =

100 for search. NRBR uses the same 𝑅 = 40. The connectivity-loss thresholds of ACTIVE are CL 1 = 1/3 and CL 2 = 1/2. Unless otherwise specified, all updates use 32 threads, and each query 𝛼 is randomly sampled from [0, 1].

Workloads . By default, we construct a DVQ index on 100% of each dataset for search and deletion experiments, and another index on 50% of each dataset for insertion experiments. For deletions, we use the 100% index and remove 1% of the vectors in each of 10 batches, resulting in a total of 10% deletions. For insertions, we use the 50% index and insert 1% of the vectors in each of 10 batches, resulting in a total of 10% insertions. 

Metrics . We measure search accuracy using Recall@ 𝑘 (𝑘 = 10 by default) and search efficiency using average query latency, while update (i.e., deletions and insertions) performance is evaluated using throughput (deletions/insertions per second).

ACTIVE achieves substantially lower latency than MR in most cases, as MR misses many objects with small weighted distances during candidate generation. On HM, ACTIVE incurs higher search latency than DEG because its neighbors are more widely dispersed in Pareto-angle space, with a mean angular difference of 16 .07 ◦, compared with 8 .73 ◦ for OI and 10 .38 ◦ for CM. This requires a larger threshold to retain useful pruning comparisons. When 𝜃 𝑡ℎ exceeds 𝜋 /6, 

ACTIVE achieves search performance competitive with DEG, as shown in Figure 11. A detailed analysis is provided in Appendix C. Notably, on CW, MR outperforms ACTIVE and DEG when 𝑘 = 10. This is because CW has low coordinate diversity, with only about 1993 unique coordinates among ∼7.2M objects. In this case, all retrieved results share the same coordinate values. Consequently, the query results are dominated by single-vector retrieval over the text, effectively reducing the search to a single-vector search. However, as 𝑘 increases, the retrieved results exhibit multiple distinct coordinate values, making the joint consideration of text and coordinate distances increasingly important. 

Impact of 𝛼 Distributions . To reflect realistic query preferences that may occur in practice, we generate three Beta distributions that favor the second attribute, treat both attributes equally, and favor the first attribute. We evaluate the accuracy–efficiency trade-off on OI, as shown in Figure 12. Pareto-frontier-based indices remain stable under all three distributions, whereas MR is highly sensitive to the 𝛼 distribution and degrades sharply when 𝛼 concentrates around 0 .5 (see Figure 12b). 

6.3 Update Performance 

We evaluate the update (i.e., deletion and insertion) performance of different methods on five real-world vector datasets, reporting the average results with standard deviation over three runs to mitigate system-level fluctuations. 

Deletion Throughput Comparison . As shown in Figure 13, 

ACTIVE consistently achieves higher throughput than both RBR and NRBR across all datasets, improving deletion throughput by 22.64–39 .51 × over RBR and 1.64–2.06 × over NRBR. The key advan-tages of ACTIVE lie in its connectivity-loss-driven adaptive repair (CA-PFR) strategy and ACAR, both of which substantially reduce the computational overhead during deletions. It is noteworthy that the throughput of ACTIVE is relatively low in the first batch, since the reverse graph needs to be explicitly initialized, whereas it can be maintained asynchronously in subsequent batches. 

Insertion Throughput Comparison . As shown in Figure 14, 

ACTIVE improves insertion throughput by 1 .20–1.43 × compared with the incremental construction of DEG. The improvement is attributed to ACAR, which reduces the number of distance computations by introducing Pareto-angle constraints. 

Throughput Variability . As shown in Figure 13 and Figure 14, the throughput gaps between ACTIVE and the baselines are consistently larger than the run-to-run variability indicated by the standard deviation error bars. 

Distance Computation Comparison . We further compare the number of distance computations of ACTIVE against other methods across all datasets, as shown in Figure 15. Under 1% deletions, 

ACTIVE consistently requires fewer computations than RBR and NRBR, reducing the computation count by 8.72 ×–38 .70 × over RBR and by 1 .70 ×–2.53 × over NRBR. This is attributed to the fact that CA-PFR adaptively selects different repair strategies for each affected node instead of applying a fixed repair strategy, even when the connectivity loss 𝐶𝐿 of the affected node is small. Under 1% insertions, ACTIVE reduces the number of computations compared to DEG, achieving a reduction of 1 .23 ×–1.43 ×, thanks to ACAR. 

6.4 Index Quality 

Although all designs in ACTIVE substantially improve update per-formance, it is necessary to evaluate whether ACTIVE can maintain graph index quality during updates. To this end, we measure search accuracy and average search latency (ms) of different methods under 1% deletions and 1% insertions. 

Search Accuracy Comparison under deletions . As shown in Figure 16, compared with RBR, ACTIVE achieves comparable recall (with a Recall@10 gap ranging from −1.23% to +0.49%) across most datasets, indicating that our local adaptive repair strategy can closely match the effectiveness of global reconstruction for affected nodes. On HM, RBR achieves higher search accuracy than 

ACTIVE , but with 30 .28 × slower deletion throughput. The recall gap arises because local repair in ACTIVE cannot always recover Pareto frontiers as accurate as those of RBR. Compared with NRBR, 

ACTIVE improves search accuracy by 0.21%–2 .03%. 

Search Accuracy Comparison under Insertions . Figure 17 shows that ACTIVE achieves recall comparable to that of DEG across all datasets (with a Recall@10 gap ranging from −0.13% to +0.04%), indicating that our proposed ACAR improves the AR computation efficiency while maintaining search accuracy closely matching the baseline.

To further assess the impact of different update methods on search performance, we measure the average search latency on the largest dataset, LN, separately under deletions and insertions. As shown in Figure 18, ACTIVE achieves search latency comparable to that of other methods and remains consistently stable under both deletions and insertions. These results show that ACAR and CA-PFR improve update per-formance while keeping index quality comparable to the baselines. 

6.5 Update Stability 

We also evaluate the stability of update performance under stream-ing data on OI. Specifically, we set the sliding window size to cover the first 50% of the dataset and use these nodes to build the initial index. In each batch of updates, the window slides forward by 1% of the dataset, i.e., we insert 1% of the remaining data and delete 1% of the data from the beginning of the window. 

Long-Term Update Stability . We repeat the sliding-window update process 50 times, by which point the entire index has been re-placed and a completely new index has been constructed. Figure 19a shows that all methods maintain stable update performance, and 

ACTIVE consistently retains a clear advantage. We further evaluate search accuracy after each update, as shown in Figure 19b. ACTIVE 

achieves search accuracy comparable to other baselines. 

Mixed Reader/Writer Workload . We evaluate queries under concurrent updates on the OI index, with 16 update threads contin-uously performing sliding-window updates and 16 query threads issuing search requests in parallel. We record the p50, p95, and p99 query latencies under continuously batched updates and show the first 300 seconds of the trace for clarity. As shown in Figure 20, 

ACTIVE achieves lower query latency than the other baselines under continuous batch updates. Notably, all methods exhibit periodic latency drops. This occurs because, between consecutive update batches and between insertion and deletion within a single batch, read–write lock contention is briefly released and query threads face less competition for CPU and memory bandwidth. 

6.6 Scalability 

We evaluate deletion and insertion performance on the OI dataset under different batch sizes to assess scalability with respect to update granularity. 

Throughput under Different Batch Sizes . As shown in Fig-ure 21a and 21b, when the batch size increases from 0.1% to 10% of the dataset, all methods achieve higher update throughput. This is because larger batch updates amortize fixed system overheads, thereby improving overall throughput. Notably, ACTIVE consis-tently outperforms all baselines across different batch sizes under both deletions and insertions, indicating that our proposed ACAR and CA-PFR provide a consistent performance advantage across a wide range of update granularity. 

Search Accuracy under Different Batch Sizes . Figure 21c shows that as batch size increases, recall of ACTIVE and RBR improves while NRBR degrades, indicating that NRBR fails to repair con-nectivity loss under large-batch deletions. ACTIVE achieves recall comparable to RBR across all batch sizes. Figure 21d shows that 

ACTIVE consistently achieves search accuracy comparable to DEG across all batch sizes, validating the effectiveness of ACAR. 

6.7 Parameter Sensitivity 

In ACTIVE , update performance is mainly affected by three pa-rameters, namely the Pareto angle threshold 𝜃 𝑡ℎ in ACAR, and the connectivity loss thresholds 𝐶𝐿 1 and 𝐶𝐿 2 in CA-PFR. We next study the impact of these parameters on update throughput and recall by varying them, and motivate the choice of the default settings. 

Pareto Angle Threshold . In ACAR, a larger 𝜃 𝑡ℎ allows each candidate node to be compared with more previously retained nodes, resulting in lower efficiency of the AR computation. To evaluate its impact, we conduct a sensitivity analysis on OI under 1% deletions and insertions by varying 𝜃 𝑡ℎ among 𝜋 /18, 𝜋 /6, 5 𝜋 /18, 7𝜋 /18, and 𝜋 /2, as shown in Figure 22. The results show that 

𝜃 𝑡ℎ = 𝜋 /18 achieves the highest throughput on both insertion and deletion, with only a small loss in Recall@10 relative to larger 

𝜃 𝑡ℎ values. Therefore, we set 𝜃 𝑡ℎ to 𝜋 /18 by default. 

Connectivity Loss Thresholds . We further evaluate joint CL 1 ×

CL 2 settings on OI. Figure 23 shows that the default setting CL 1 =

1/3 and CL 2 = 1/2 provides a consistent throughput–accuracy trade-off. Compared with the highest-recall setting (CL 1 = CL 2 =

1/3), it improves deletion throughput by 10 .28% with only 0 .07% lower Recall@10. Compared with the highest-throughput setting

Tuning Guidance . We recommend using the default parameters of ACTIVE as the first choice. They are empirical default values obtained from experiments across different datasets, different up-date batch sizes, different 𝛼 distributions, and different update patterns. For datasets or workloads that require fine-tuning, one can run experiments similar to those in Figure 22 and Figure 23 on randomly sampled dual-vector data to select more suitable parameters. Specifically, increasing 𝜃 𝑡ℎ improves search accuracy but increases the cost of active range computation. For CL 1 and CL 2,we recommend adjusting CL 1 first to obtain a better throughput– accuracy trade-off for the current workload.

to RBR. Each component yields consistent speedups across batch sizes. Specifically, we first introduce the connectivity-loss-driven adaptive repair algorithm (+C.A.), which adaptively repairs affected nodes according to the degree of connectivity loss, achieving average speedups of 13.85 ×, 12.77 ×, and 11.34 × under the three batch sizes, respectively. We then further incorporate an asyn-chronously maintained reverse graph (+Async.), increasing the average speedups to 19.46 ×, 14.95 ×, and 12.27 ×, respectively, by avoiding scanning the entire graph topology. Finally, we introduce the angle-constrained AR computation algorithm (+A.C.), improv-ing the average speedups to 25.76 ×, 25.50 ×, and 18.05 ×, respectively. Notably, the asynchronously maintained reverse graph provides significant performance gains under the 0.1% batch size. Its main benefit is eliminating full graph scans, whereas the cost of in-memory access is relatively small.

Figure 25: Ablation studies of CA-PFR and ACAR. Ablation of CA-PFR . We compare deletion throughput and Recall@10 for four threshold settings on OI after 90 batches of 1% deletions. The first uses CL 1 = CL 2 = 1 (only Mild), where all affected nodes are repaired as mild loss. The second uses CL 1 = 1/3and CL 2 = 1 (+Moderate), which yields only mild and moderate loss. The third uses CL 1 = 1/3 and CL 2 = 1/2 (+Severe), which is the full three-level CA-PFR. As shown in Figure 25a, the full strategy (+Severe) achieves the best overall trade-off. Although the first strategy achieves higher throughput, it fails to maintain graph connectivity under sustained deletions. Compared with the forth strategy, which uses CL 1 = 1/3 and CL 2 = 1/3 (Mild/Severe), CA-PFR achieves 7.51% higher deletion throughput with only a 0.03% decrease in recall. 

Ablation of ACAR . To examine whether the first Pareto-frontier layer requires special treatment (FL), we compare the full ACAR with a variant without this treatment (ACAR w/o FL), which applies the same angle-constrained procedure uniformly to all layers, including the first layer. As shown in Figure 25b, the full ACAR consistently achieves a better accuracy-efficiency trade-off.

7 RELATED WORK 

Hybrid Search . To meet the demands of increasingly complex real-world applications, various hybrid search paradigms have been proposed, including filtered ANNS [36, 45, 54, 64] and multi-vector ANNS [48]. Filtered ANNS associates each object with both vector representations and structured attributes, supporting approximate nearest neighbor search under attribute constraints such as numerical ranges [15, 25, 27, 37, 53, 58, 66], temporal conditions [52], and categorical filters [8, 17, 56]. Multi-vector ANNS represents each object with multiple embeddings and jointly optimizes similarity across vector spaces [6, 10, 14, 40, 41, 61]. These paradigms extend traditional ANNS by incorporating structured or multi-view semantic information. 

Dual-Vector Query . Existing dual-vector query approaches fall into two categories: preference-specific multi-index methods [48, 63] and preference-agnostic unified index methods [61]. The for-mer fails to maintain high search accuracy under arbitrary query preferences, while the latter achieves a better accuracy–efficiency trade-off but does not support efficient updates. 

Chamfer-based Multi-Vector Retrieval (CMVR) . The similarity between objects in CMVR [14] is measured by CHAMFER (𝑄, 𝑃 ) =

Í𝑞 𝑖 ∈𝑄 max 𝑝 𝑗 ∈𝑃 ⟨𝑞 𝑖 , 𝑝 𝑗 ⟩, where 𝑃 and 𝑄 denote the document and query vector sets, respectively. CMVR can capture finer-grained semantic information within a single feature than traditional 𝐿 2 or cosine distance measures applied to single-vector representations. This setting differs substantially from DVQ in both the retrieval task and the similarity measure, and therefore CMVR methods, such as MUVERA [14], cannot be used directly in DVQ tasks. 

Graph-based Index Updates . In single-vector graph-based in-dices, dynamic updates [18, 28, 57, 62] have been extensively studied. Insertions are typically performed via incremental con-struction [28, 47, 62], and recent work such as ParlayANN [31] further accelerates this process through scalable and deterministic parallel batch insertion. Deletions are handled by either global reinsertion [30, 60] or local neighbor reconnection [47, 62]. 

8 CONCLUSION 

We propose ACTIVE , a dynamic Pareto-frontier-based unified DVQ index that supports efficient updates while maintaining comparable retrieval quality under arbitrary query preferences. To accelerate index construction and insertions, we design an angle-constrained active range computation algorithm, ACAR, which reduces distance computations via Pareto-angle-based constraints. To support efficient updates, we further propose a connectivity-loss-driven adaptive repair algorithm (CA-PFR) that selects different repair strategies based on the connectivity loss of affected nodes. Experiments demonstrate that ACTIVE achieves a strong trade-off between retrieval quality and update throughput across datasets.

A APPLICABILITY TO OTHER DUAL ATTRIBUTES 

Datasets with Additional Dual Attributes . ACTIVE is not limited to image–text data, but supports arbitrary combinations of data types. To further examine the applicability of ACTIVE , we add two geo-tagged datasets, as shown in Table 3. The first is Regions (RS) [1], a multilingual geotagged social-media corpus collected from Twitter, where each text post is embedded using BERT [13]. The second is MP16-Pro (MP) [24], a geo-tagged image collection from Flickr, where each image is embedded into a 768-dimensional vector using DINOv2 ViT-B/14 [35]. We conduct both static search and dynamic update experiments on RS and MP.

Static Search Performance . The accuracy-efficiency trade-off results of ACTIVE , DEG, and MR on RS and MP are shown in Figure 27. Under the same search latency, the Recall@10 of ACTIVE 

is on average 0 .83% and 0 .32% lower than that of DEG on RS and MP, respectively. Meanwhile, ACTIVE substantially outperforms MR, improving Recall@10 by 33 .10% on RS and by 15 .17% on MP under the same latency. These results show that Pareto-frontier-based indices remain effective for text-coordinate and image-coordinate attribute pairs, and that ACTIVE preserves search quality close to DEG while clearly surpassing multi-index retrieval. B ANALYSIS OF AFFECTED NODES 

By default, ACTIVE treats in-neighbors of deleted nodes as af-fected nodes, since deletions mainly cause connectivity loss of in-neighbors. We argue that repairing only in-neighbors is sufficient to largely restore connectivity. To validate this, we compare ACTIVE 

(In) with two variants on OI under 1% batch deletions. ACTIVE (Out) repairs only out-neighbors, while ACTIVE (In+Out) repairs both in-neighbors and out-neighbors of deleted nodes. As shown in Figure 32, ACTIVE (In) consistently achieves higher update throughput and better search accuracy than other repair strategies. Figure 32: Impact of different affected node definitions. 15 C SENSITIVITY ANALYSIS OF THE PARETO ANGLE THRESHOLD 𝜃 𝑡ℎ 

To understand why HM is more sensitive to the Pareto angle thresh-old 𝜃 𝑡ℎ , we analyze the Pareto angle dispersion of its neighbors and the local neighborhood consistency between its two attribute spaces. 

Pareto Angle Dispersion . We analyze the distribution of dual-attribute distances between each node 𝑢 and its neighbors, as shown in Figure 33. Specifically, for each node 𝑢 , we collect the distance pairs (𝛿 𝑥 (𝑢, 𝑣 ), 𝛿 𝑦 (𝑢, 𝑣 )) for all its neighbors 𝑣 and aggregate them across all nodes to characterize the overall neighbor distribution of each dataset. HM exhibits a wider Pareto-angle interval containing 95% of the neighbor pairs, spanning 55 .5◦, compared with 31 .0◦ for OI and 43 .0◦ for CM. To further quantify the dispersion of neighbors, we compute the average difference in Pareto angles among the neighbors of each node and average it across all nodes. Under the same maximum neighbor count 𝑅 , HM exhibits a substantially larger mean angular difference of 16 .07 ◦, compared with 8 .73 ◦ for OI and 10 .38 ◦ for CM. These results indicate that the neighbors of individual nodes in HM tend to be more widely spread in the Pareto angular space. Consequently, a small threshold may exclude more potentially useful pruning comparisons in HM, affecting neighbor selection quality and search performance. 0 0.5 1

Figure 33: Distribution of dual-attribute distances between nodes and their neighbors. The blue dashed rays delimit the shortest continuous Pareto-angle interval containing 95% of the neighbor pairs. The angular width of each interval is annotated. Local Neighborhood Consistency . To understand the data prop-erties underlying the differences in Pareto-angle distributions, we measure local neighborhood consistency directly from the attribute vectors, independently of the graph index. We uniformly sample 10,000 objects from each dataset and compute their exact nearest-neighbor rankings over the entire dataset, excluding the source object itself. For each sampled object, we identify its 100 nearest neighbors in attribute space 𝑥 and calculate their average distance-rank percentile in attribute space 𝑦 . We then average these values across all sampled objects. As shown in Table 4, HM has a mean percentile of 49 .99%, close to the expected percentile of approxi-mately 50% for uniformly random candidates. In contrast, OI and CM have lower mean percentiles of 38 .98% and 32 .90%, respectively, indicating stronger local neighborhood consistency between the two attribute spaces. HM’s weaker consistency, together with its greater Pareto angular dispersion, helps explain why it is more sensitive to the threshold.
